attempts.raw_response: The first English Reclaim the Night march took place in 1977 in Leeds, followed by London later that same year. These marches emerged directly from the consciousness-raising groups of the Women's Liberation Movement, which sought to name and challenge the systemic nature of male violence against women. Organisers deliberately chose to march at night, challenging the notion that women should restrict their movements after dark for safety. The marches became annual events in cities across Britain throughout the late 1970s and 1980s, with participants holding candles and torches while chanting slogans such as "We want the streets back at night." The movement also connected to broader demands for better police responses to sexual assault and for funding for women's refuges and support services.

pair.human_continuation:
On 30 April 1977 in Germany, synchronised marches took place in several cities, protesting against rape and violence against women. In July 1977, the idea of UK marches was discussed at a conference on Radical Feminism in Edinburgh. Feminists from Leeds were present at the conference and the Leeds Revolutionary Feminist Group organised the first Reclaim the Night marches. One of the co-founders of the 1977 march was Al Garthwaite, who later became a Leeds councillor.

Marches in Leeds in 1977 
The first Reclaim the Night protests took place in Leeds on 12 November 1977. The marches were in part a response to the "Yorkshire Ripper" murders, and the police response which instructed women to stay out of public spaces after dark.

History 

The Reclaim the Night marches were part of the Women's Liberation Movement in England. The inspiration came from a march held in Brussels in 1976, which, according to historian Finn Mackay, was the "first documented incidence of an organised, urban, women's night-time march against male violence against women".
